Priming / Narrative Seeding.short_definition: Planting an interpretation of a person or event in someone's mind ahead of time, so that what they later see gets read through it.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.expanded_definition: Priming, or narrative seeding, is the quiet handing over of a conclusion before the evidence arrives. A remark in the hallway, a story told before a visit, a heads-up before a meeting: each sets a lens, and the later event is read through it. One warning from a friend who cares may be only that. What makes it worth noticing is the order, with the frame placed first and the facts second, and later events that keep landing on the same reading. From one message you usually cannot tell, because you cannot see what was said before.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.plain_language_summary: Someone tells you what to think about a person or event before you have seen it yourself, and then what you see seems to prove it.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.why_this_matters: You read an event through a lens you never chose and mistake a supplied conclusion for your own judgement. The frame is hardest to question because it arrived before the evidence did, so by the time you look, you already know what you expect to see.
what_it_is: A remark placed just before an encounter: 'Just so you know, she can get prickly' said as you walk into a meeting with her.
A story told before a visit, hearing, interview or first date that tells you how to read the person you are about to meet.
A matter of order: the interpretation comes first, so ordinary behavior afterward gets sorted as confirming it.
Aimed at a person, a group, a decision or an incident, and it can be flattering as well as unflattering.
Often invisible to the person it works on, who remembers forming the opinion themselves.
Different from a briefing, which hands over facts and leaves the reading to you.
what_it_sounds_like: Not to prejudice you, but you'll see what I mean when you meet him.
Just a heads-up before the meeting: she tends to take things personally.
I'm sure it's nothing, but keep an eye on how he reacts when money comes up.
You'll notice she goes quiet when something is off.
A relative describes your partner to the whole family before the first dinner, in a tone of concern.
A new manager's first week opens with a colleague's three-minute account of who to be careful around.
Everyone says the last team lead was awful, so watch how this one handles it.
what_it_is_not: A briefing that gives you facts you can check, such as a colleague telling you the client moved the deadline twice last month.
A sincere warning from someone who had a bad experience and presents it as their experience, not as a fact about the person.
Reading someone through your own history with them, which is memory and not a frame handed to you.
A reputation that formed because many people independently reported the same thing.
A hunch you formed yourself from earlier meetings.
Ordinary scene-setting, such as a host mentioning that Grandpa is hard of hearing so you speak up.
this_may_be_it_when: The comment arrives just before an encounter, instead of when something relevant came up.
It tells you how to interpret behavior ('watch how she reacts') rather than describing something that happened.
Afterward you notice exactly the behavior you were told to expect, and little else.
The same advance word is given to several people who will all be in the room.
Asked what the comment was based on, the speaker has no specific event to point to.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker can describe a specific event, with a date, and you can check it yourself.
They tell you in the same breath what the other person does well.
They say 'ignore me if it turns out differently' and then actually let it.
You had formed the same impression on your own before hearing anything.
The remark is practical information about the setting, such as parking, deadlines or who has authority to decide.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People pass on context because they care about you and want the first meeting to go smoothly.
Someone nervous about an encounter may rehearse their own worries aloud, and the listener hears a verdict.
Gossip travels through habit as much as design, and the speaker may not notice how it shapes the listener.
Many workplaces hand over notes about people as routine, so a heads-up may be a handover habit.
common_false_positives: A nurse's shift handover noting that a patient was agitated overnight, shared so the next shift can help.
A friend warning you that the restaurant you picked is very loud, so you can set your expectations.
Your own past with someone coloring how you read their next message, with nobody having said a word.
discernment_questions: What did I know about this person or event before I saw it, and who told me?
Would I have reached this reading if I had arrived with no advance word?
Was the comment a fact I could check, or an instruction about how to interpret?
Does everything I have seen since fit so neatly that I have stopped looking for anything that does not?
Did the person who told me also say what they were basing it on?
less_concerning_if: The advance word named something specific and checkable, and you checked it.
The speaker also offered the other side, or said they might be wrong.
You went in curious, and your impression changed once you met the person.
more_concerning_if: The same advance word is delivered to everyone who will meet the person, before they meet.
Anyone who reports something different from the frame is told they are being naive.
The person being described never learns what was said about them, though decisions about them follow.
pattern_over_time_signs: Before each new encounter with the same person, a similar piece of advance commentary appears.
New people join a group already holding a view of someone they have never spoken to.
The person described meets wariness they cannot trace to anything they did.
Your own impression has drifted toward the advance description, and you can no longer say which part came from experience.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.repair_check: Repair here means going back to the people who were given the frame and correcting it: saying what was opinion, what was fact, and what is not known. Quietly dropping the subject, while the earlier framing stays in everyone's head, leaves the lens in place.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself what happens when you say you would like to form your own view. A reply like 'fair enough', followed by a change in how they talk, suggests the request was heard. More advance commentary, now with a note that you are naive, suggests it was not.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.psychological_mechanism: People tend to look for what they were told to expect. Once a story is in place, ambiguous behavior can be sorted into it and contrary behavior explained away as an exception. Because the story arrived as information and not as pressure, the listener may remember adopting it freely. It tends to work better when the source is trusted and the encounter is unfamiliar.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe walking into a room already wary, then feeling puzzled at how readily a stranger's behavior seemed to match the warning. Some say they later realized their first impression had never really been tested. A person described in advance can meet coolness they cannot explain, and may start changing how they act to shake it off.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask where it comes from: 'What did you see that makes you say that?' A specific answer is something you can weigh, and a vague one tells you how much weight to give it.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will form your own view: 'Thanks, but I'd rather meet him without a briefing.'
response_options.disengagement: Change the subject when advance commentary starts, and let the meeting itself be the first evidence you collect.
response_options.support_seeking: If you are the one being described, ask a trusted colleague or friend what has been said about you and who said it, so you know what to expect before you arrive.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for facts in writing before a meeting about a person: dates, documents, who was there. Raise it with a manager or HR if opinions about someone are circulating before they can respond.

Priming / Narrative Seeding.boundary_script: "I appreciate the heads-up, but I'd like to meet her without it. If something specific happened, tell me what and when, and I'll weigh it myself. Otherwise I'll make up my own mind."
Priming / Narrative Seeding.safety_note: Rarely a safety concern alone. It changes when advance word is aimed at people who control something you depend on, such as a landlord, an employer, a custody evaluator or an immigration officer, or arrives with threats or isolation. Then write down what was said and by whom, and take it to a legal aid service or an advocate before you respond.
misuse_warning: Any advance warning can be called seeding. Treating every heads-up as a plot leaves you unable to take sincere advice, and the label cannot show what anyone meant.
Suspecting that someone primed your friends can become its own lens, in which every cool reception proves the plot.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Credibility Theft aims advance word at one thing, whether you can be believed as a witness; priming can set any interpretation, including of an event, and does not need to attack anyone's honesty. Frame Assassination swaps out a frame in the middle of a conversation, while priming places one before the conversation starts. Authority Hijack tells you what you feel, whereas priming tells you what you will see in someone else.
Priming / Narrative Seeding.core_meaning: Planting an interpretation of a person or event in someone's mind ahead of time, so that what they later see gets read through it.

Credibility Theft.short_definition: Casting doubt on someone's reliability in advance, so whatever they later report is heard as doubtful before they have said it.
Credibility Theft.expanded_definition: Credibility theft works on the audience, not on the argument. Remarks about someone's memory, mood, honesty or habit of exaggerating are placed with people who have not yet heard their account: relatives, coworkers, a manager, a school. When the account arrives, it is weighed against the reputation instead of the facts. Doubting a single claim is not this. The pattern is doubt about the person, spread early and widely, without any specific claim being named.
Credibility Theft.plain_language_summary: Before you have said anything, other people have been told you exaggerate, get confused or are hard to believe, so what you report lands already doubted.
Credibility Theft.why_this_matters: Your account is discounted before you give it, so whatever you later report meets people who have already been prepared not to believe it, and you may never find out why. Asking for help becomes hardest exactly when you most need it.
what_it_is: Remarks about your reliability that reach other people before your own account does, such as 'she remembers things her own way.'
Aimed at the person, not a claim: no particular statement is named as wrong, only that you are the kind of person who gets things wrong.
Often built on real moments of weakness, such as a tearful day, an old mistake or a diagnosis, offered as proof you cannot be relied on.
Found in family group chats, workplaces, schools, custody and housing disputes, and wherever someone will later decide whose account to believe.
Different from Gaslighting, which works on your trust in your own memory; this works on other people's trust in you.
what_it_sounds_like: You know how she exaggerates.
I'm not saying he's lying, just that he gets confused about dates.
Take what she says with a pinch of salt, she's been going through a lot.
Don't be surprised if he tells you a different story; he does that.
Your manager has already been told you 'tend to misread situations' before you raise your concern.
When you report something, the reply opens with 'is this another one of your situations?'
A relative tells the others, 'She'll probably bring that up again, just be kind about it.'
what_it_is_not: A documented record of inaccuracy reasonably affects how much weight an account carries, and doubting one particular claim is not a campaign. The separation is between doubt about a claim and doubt installed in advance about the person.
A colleague saying 'I'm not sure about that date, can we check the email?'
Mutual wariness between two people who have each been caught out before.
A private word to you, from someone who cares, that you seem overwhelmed lately.
An investigator or judge testing a witness's account, which is their job.
Someone honestly disagreeing with what you said and telling you so in the open.
this_may_be_it_when: People you have not yet told anything already seem to hold a version of you.
The doubt names no particular claim and has no example attached.
Something you reported gets a reply about your state of mind and not about what you reported.
The remarks about you come from one source and travel along the same line of people.
The doubts are raised mostly around times you are about to speak, complain or ask for help.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The doubt is tied to a specific, checkable mistake, which the speaker also names to you.
The same people trust you on other matters and have been told nothing about you.
Your account is checked against records and holds up, with no change in how you are treated.
The person who raised concerns about your reliability said it to you first.
Skepticism is applied equally to everyone's reports, including the speaker's own.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Past mistakes honestly reduce how much people rely on someone, and nobody needs to be working on that.
A worried relative may talk to others about your health out of care, not to weaken what you say.
People rank claims by how well the source has done before, which is an ordinary habit.
common_false_positives: A finance reviewer asking for receipts before accepting an expense claim, as they do for all staff.
A judge or investigator testing everyone's testimony.
A friend who teases you about always being late and then believes you when you say the train was delayed.
discernment_questions: Can I trace anything said about me to a specific claim I made that was wrong?
Did people seem to doubt me before I had said anything?
Do those who doubt me share a single source?
Does the same doubt appear for every topic, or only when I am complaining?
Would a record, such as dated messages or documents, back my account if someone looked?
less_concerning_if: The doubt is limited to one claim and is settled by looking at the evidence.
Everyone's accounts get checked, not only yours.
You can learn what has been said about you, and you are given the chance to respond.
more_concerning_if: You are not told what has been said about you, even though decisions about you follow.
A health condition, past mistake or hard period is mentioned to people who have no need to know.
A formal report you made is received with the reputation first and the content second.
pattern_over_time_signs: Reports you make start to be met with remarks about you as a person, not about the matter.
You hear from third parties that you were described as 'dramatic' or 'unreliable' before you ever met them.
You begin to leave out things you know to be true because you expect not to be believed.
More and more, you need a witness or a document before anyone will take you seriously.
Credibility Theft.repair_check: Repair would mean going back to the people who were given the doubt and correcting what they were told, naming what was fact and what was opinion. An apology made only to you, with the earlier remarks left standing among everyone else, has not reached where the damage is.
Credibility Theft.boundary_respect_check: Ask to know who has been told what, and watch whether you get an answer. A response that names the people and the words, and stops there, is a response to your request. A response that questions why you want to know is a response to something else.
Credibility Theft.psychological_mechanism: People often judge a report by the reputation of whoever makes it, since checking every claim takes effort. An early remark about unreliability hands listeners a shortcut: they can disbelieve without examining. It tends to work better when it contains something true, like a bad week, and comes from someone the listener already trusts. The person it describes may begin to doubt themselves too.
Credibility Theft.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe being met with polite doubt when they report something important, and learning later what had been said. Some hold back reports, over-prepare evidence, or avoid the people who may have heard the remarks. A lonely sense of being right and unheard is also reported, along with exhaustion at having to prove ordinary things.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask directly what was said: 'I've heard you've described me as unreliable. Can you tell me what you had in mind?' Keep it a question, and write down the answer afterward.
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask to be heard on the facts: 'Please judge what I'm reporting by the evidence, not by what you've heard about me. I can show you the messages.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to win each doubter over one at a time. Put your account in writing, with dates, and let the record speak where conversation cannot.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell one person who knew you before this began what has been said, and ask whether it matches how they know you. Their answer helps you test the doubt you may have absorbed.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, keep a dated file of what you reported and what happened, and ask HR or a union representative how to put your concerns on record. Quiet documentation counts for more than an argument.

Credibility Theft.boundary_script: "I'd like what I report to be looked at on its own facts. I have messages and dates for it. Could we go through them together, or could someone else look at them with us?"
Credibility Theft.safety_note: This often travels with bigger problems. Watch for doubt being planted with people who decide things about you, such as a landlord, employer, family court or doctor, and for remarks about your mental state used to explain away a report of harm. Keep dated copies somewhere only you can reach, and speak to a legal aid service or an advocate before the next formal step.
misuse_warning: Anyone whose account was doubted can feel this has happened to them. A record of real errors reasonably lowers trust, and using the label to wave that record away turns it around.
Confronting the people who repeated the remarks as if they had planned them can look like one more attempt to discredit someone. Check what was actually said, and by whom, before you describe it.
Credibility Theft.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Gaslighting works on your own trust in your memory, in private; Credibility Theft works on other people's trust in you, usually out of your hearing. Priming / Narrative Seeding sets any interpretation before an encounter, while this one targets your reliability as a witness. Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing relies on clinical labels; this tactic needs no label at all, only the suggestion that you are not to be taken at your word.
Credibility Theft.core_meaning: Casting doubt on someone's reliability in advance, so whatever they later report is heard as doubtful before they have said it.

Projection.short_definition: Charging someone with a behavior or motive that the exchange shows more clearly in the person making the charge.
Projection.expanded_definition: A classic idea in psychology is that people can attribute their own feelings or impulses to someone else, often without realizing it. In everyday conflict this looks like an accusation that fits the accuser better than the accused: 'You're so controlling' said in the middle of a list of instructions. It does not show what anyone meant, and people can do it unknowingly. One mismatch is ordinary. The pattern is a repeated one, where the charges track whatever you just pointed out.
Projection.plain_language_summary: You say something is happening, and you are told you are the one doing it, even though the record fits the other person more.
Projection.why_this_matters: You spend the conversation defending yourself against the very thing you came to name, which makes the source of the harm hard to see, and harder to describe to anyone else. The conflict ends in a tie instead of an answer.
what_it_is: An accusation that hands your complaint back in nearly the same words: 'You never listen' answered with 'No, you never listen.'
Often arrives right after you name a behavior, not at some random time.
Can be sincere and unaware: someone may truly not see the behavior in themselves while seeing it clearly in you.
Judged by the record, not the tone: dated messages, who said what, and whether the charge matches what is on the page.
Different from fair mutual criticism, where both people can say 'yes, we both do that.'
what_it_sounds_like: You're the one who's controlling, said by someone who has just told you whom you may see.
I'm not angry, you're angry, said loudly.
You're always accusing me of lying. You're the liar here.
You're being so defensive! said in reply to a calm question.
You're obsessed with money, said by a person who has just reviewed every receipt.
I'm not the one who doesn't trust you. You're the one who doesn't trust me.
An email answers your note about missed deadlines with a list of deadlines you supposedly missed, none of them dated.
what_it_is_not: An accusation can be accurate even when it also describes the accuser, and in most conflicts both people contribute some of the same behavior. Someone naming a pattern they share, and owning their half, is doing the opposite.
A counter-complaint that is specific, dated and checkable, even if it is uncomfortable to hear.
A genuine mirror, where both of you do the thing and each can see it.
A flash of defensiveness that the person admits an hour later.
Honest self-reflection such as 'I think I'm stressed, and I may be hearing criticism where there is none.'
this_may_be_it_when: The charge matches what you said almost word for word.
It arrives only after you name something, never on an ordinary day.
The behavior charged is visible in that same conversation, in the person making the charge.
No example, date or message is given for the charge.
When you offer to check the record, the subject shifts.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They can point to a specific time you did it, and you recognize it.
They add 'and I do it too.'
The concern was raised before you named anything, as part of something they were already worried about.
When you show them the record, they accept what it shows.
A third person who knows you both finds the charge fair.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Anyone under stress can hear criticism as a verdict and answer with the nearest words.
Couples often argue in loops where both use the same complaints because both feel the same lack.
People notice in others what they themselves worry about, and say it aloud without any plan.
common_false_positives: Siblings who each say 'you started it' about a fight both took part in.
A manager who says 'we both need to communicate better' after a missed handover.
A friend who admits 'I do the same thing, honestly' after you pointed something out.
discernment_questions: Does the accusation fit what the record shows about them, about me, or about both of us?
Did it arrive after I named something, almost like an echo?
Could I give a specific example of my behavior that matches it, and could they give one of theirs?
When I offer to look at messages or dates together, does the subject change?
Would someone who knows us both recognize the charge as true of me?
less_concerning_if: The charge is specific enough to check, and it holds up on some points.
They accept the parts that fit and say so.
You can both name a shared habit without it turning into a contest.
more_concerning_if: The same accusation returns every time you name a behavior, whatever it is.
The record clearly shows the opposite of what you are charged with.
You have started to avoid describing any behavior for fear of hearing it said back.
pattern_over_time_signs: You rehearse complaints so that nothing in them can be turned around, and it never works.
Conversations end in a draw, each accused of the same thing and nothing settled.
You catch yourself apologizing for things you were the one to raise.
Friends who watch the pattern describe it as a mirror, and you begin doubting your own account.
Projection.repair_check: Change sounds like, 'I think you named something real, and I do it too,' followed by action. A reply that agrees in general terms and then charges you with the same thing again is the earlier exchange in a softer voice.
Projection.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself whether you can say one thing, once, and have it heard before anything is said back. If a plain statement about what happened gets a counter-statement every time, the space to finish your sentence is not being held.
Projection.psychological_mechanism: When a charge comes back at you in similar words, it can be hard to tell whether it is true. You may start searching yourself for the fault, which uses up the attention you needed to hold your point. If the accuser truly does not see the trait in themselves, they can deliver the charge with real conviction, and conviction is persuasive.
Projection.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe feeling dizzy in these talks, as if blame were passed back and forth faster than they could track. Some begin to wonder whether they are the ones doing what they named, or avoid naming anything at all. A few say every complaint begins to feel like a trap that closes on them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge what might be true, then go back to your point: 'I might do that sometimes. I'd still like to talk about what happened on Tuesday.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep to one thing at a time: 'Let's finish my concern, then I will listen to yours properly and give it the same time.'
response_options.disengagement: When the same words keep coming back to you, stop trading charges and move to something written, where wording cannot be echoed back in the moment.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the exchange to someone who knows you both and ask whether the charge sounds like you. Check it on a calm day, not in the middle of an argument.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep the facts in a dated email: what happened, when, and what you are asking for. A reply that engages with it, or one that charges you back, becomes part of the record.

Projection.boundary_script: "I'm open to hearing whether I do that, and I will listen when we get there. Right now I'm asking about what happened on Tuesday. Can we finish that first?"
Projection.safety_note: Having your concern turned back on you is a communication problem. It changes when the charges against you are used to justify checking your phone, controlling your movements or limiting your money, or when you start to fear the reaction to naming anything. If so, write down specifics privately and speak to a counselor or advocate outside the relationship.
misuse_warning: Saying 'you're projecting' to someone's honest complaint is itself the move described in Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown: it ends the conversation instead of describing it.
The word names an accusation that fits the accuser, which you can only judge from the record. Using it because a charge stung is not enough.
Projection.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Blame-Shifting moves responsibility for an event onto you, while projection hands you a specific trait or motive, often the one you just named. DARVO packs a denial, an attack and a role reversal together; projection can be only the echo. Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown uses psychological-sounding terms to stop the talk, whereas projection keeps the talk going, in a circle.
Projection.core_meaning: Charging someone with a behavior or motive that the exchange shows more clearly in the person making the charge.

Authority Hijack.short_definition: Insisting you know what another person really feels, thinks or meant better than they do, and treating their own account as the thing to be corrected.
Authority Hijack.expanded_definition: Authority Hijack is a claim to be the expert on someone else's inner life: 'You don't really feel that', 'What you actually mean is...' The disagreement stops being about what happened and becomes about who is allowed to know what you feel. A friend offering a different reading is not this, since you can decline it. The pattern is when your account is always the one up for correction and theirs never is.
Authority Hijack.plain_language_summary: Someone tells you what you really feel or mean, and your own explanation of your own mind is treated as the thing that needs fixing.
Authority Hijack.why_this_matters: You end up arguing the case for your own feelings, and simply being taken at your word is no longer on offer. Over time you may start checking your inner states against someone else's reading before you trust them.
what_it_is: A statement about your inner state made as fact: 'You're not angry, you're jealous.'
A rewrite of what you said: 'What you meant was...' after you have already said what you meant.
Treats your report as a draft to be edited, while the other person's reading is final.
Seen in friendships, families, workplaces and clinics, wherever one person holds some standing over another.
Different from a question: 'Could part of it be envy?' leaves you the last word.
what_it_sounds_like: You don't actually feel that, you just think you do.
I know what you really meant.
You're not upset about the meeting. You're upset about your mother.
Deep down you want me to say sorry.
I understand you better than you understand yourself.
You say you're fine, but I can tell you aren't, and I know why.
A supervisor's feedback form lists your 'real motivation' for a decision you explained in writing.
what_it_is_not: People who know you well sometimes offer a reading you had not considered, and in therapy that questioning is invited, not imposed; a clarifying question is not a counter-claim. The difference is whether your own account is still allowed to be the last word.
A friend saying 'I wonder if you're more tired than angry' and then accepting 'no, I'm angry.'
Someone noticing your behavior has changed and asking what is going on.
A guess at your mood from a visible sign, such as asking if you are cold when you are shivering.
A coach or teacher pointing out a habit you had not noticed, like rushing your answers.
A formal assessment you agreed to, in which a professional describes patterns in your answers.
this_may_be_it_when: Your stated feeling is treated as a mistaken first draft.
You have said 'that's not what I meant' and been told what you meant anyway.
The other person's reading is never offered as a question.
It happens when your feelings are inconvenient for them, such as when you are hurt by something they did.
You end up arguing about what you feel instead of about what happened.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Their reading is offered as a question and dropped once you answer.
They say 'I could be wrong' and visibly mean it.
The reading is about visible behavior and not about your inner state.
You asked for their view of what you might be feeling.
The person has nothing riding on what you feel.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who care about you often guess at your feelings and misjudge, because they want to help.
Some families speak for each other as a habit of closeness.
A well-meaning person may mix up 'I would feel that way' with 'you feel that way.'
common_false_positives: A friend who gently asks whether the real problem is the deadline and not the coworker, then accepts your answer.
A therapist's interpretation within an agreed session, offered tentatively and open to your rejection.
A parent telling a toddler 'you're tired, not hungry', which is often right for small children.
discernment_questions: When I say what I feel, is it accepted, or is it up for correction?
Is their reading offered as a question or asserted as fact?
Does it happen when my feelings are inconvenient to them?
Do I find myself checking my own feelings against their account?
If I said 'no, that's not it', would that be the last word?
less_concerning_if: The reading is a question and drops when you decline it.
It is offered only when you ask for an outside perspective.
Their interpretation is about your behavior, and your account of your reasons stands.
more_concerning_if: The reading is repeated after you have declined it more than once.
Your feelings are declared untrue mainly when they concern something the other person did.
Other people are told what you 'really' feel, so your own words are discounted.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself saying 'I think I feel' where you used to say 'I feel.'
You rehearse justifications for feelings you should not have to justify.
You catch yourself asking the other person what you must be feeling.
You share less of what is going on inside, because sharing only starts the correction.
Authority Hijack.repair_check: Repair looks like a reading becoming a question and staying one: 'Is it more this, or that?' followed by accepting your answer. Apologizing once for 'assuming' and then telling you your real motive again next week is the same claim in new clothes.
Authority Hijack.boundary_respect_check: Try stating what you feel in one short sentence, then stop. Watch who gets the last word. If your sentence stands, your boundary was heard. If it gets a second sentence explaining what you really mean, it was not.
Authority Hijack.psychological_mechanism: Few of us have perfect access to our own motives, so a confident outside reading can sound plausible. When it comes from someone close or with standing, such as a parent, partner or boss, it can be easier to adopt than to resist. Repeated, it can teach a person to look to others for the answer to what they feel.
Authority Hijack.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe being unable to say what they feel without it being corrected, and then feeling unsure of the feeling itself. Some become guarded and share less. Some say they began asking others what they must be feeling, which they later found disorienting. There can also be a flat anger at not being believed about their own mind.

response_options.soft_clarification: Give your account once, plainly: 'I do feel angry. I'm telling you how it is for me.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Mark where the authority sits: 'You can tell me how it looks from outside, but what I feel is mine to say.'
response_options.disengagement: If your feelings keep being corrected, share them less in that setting and keep them where you can hear them clearly, such as a journal or a friend.
response_options.support_seeking: Say your feeling aloud to someone with no stake and notice whether it sounds true to you in their company. Being listened to helps you hear yourself.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, put your reasons for a decision in writing, in your own words, so a manager's later account of your 'real motive' can be set beside it.

Authority Hijack.boundary_script: "If you're curious what I feel, ask me and I'll tell you. I'm not looking for a reading of it. What I've told you is what's true for me."
Authority Hijack.safety_note: Being told what you really feel is a dispute over who gets to describe your inner life. It deserves closer attention when the 'correction' is used to override your refusals, your consent or your account of being hurt. If you feel pressed toward something you have said no to, speak to a trusted person or an advocate outside the relationship before agreeing to anything.
misuse_warning: Saying 'you can't know what I feel' to shut down any honest observation turns a defense into a wall. Others sometimes see patterns you cannot, and you can listen without agreeing.
Using the label for anyone who offers an interpretation can hurt people who are trying to help.
Authority Hijack.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotional Invalidation tells you your feeling is wrong or too much; Authority Hijack tells you that you do not have the feeling you say you have. Gaslighting disputes what happened, while this one disputes what is going on inside you. Credibility Theft works on how others see your reliability, where this one works on how you are told to see yourself.
Authority Hijack.core_meaning: Insisting you know what another person really feels, thinks or meant better than they do, and treating their own account as the thing to be corrected.

Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.short_definition: Answering a complaint about someone's conduct by suggesting the complainant has a condition, so the complaint is treated as a symptom.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.expanded_definition: A complaint is raised, such as a missed diagnosis, a harsh remark or an unsafe workplace. The reply does not say whether it happened. It turns to the complainant: perhaps you are anxious, or stressed, or should talk to someone. Concern for your wellbeing can be genuine. What marks this pattern is where the matter ends: the diagnosis becomes the answer, and the complaint is never examined. It appears in families, workplaces, schools, clinics and services.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.plain_language_summary: You say something went wrong, and the reply is that maybe something is wrong with you, so what you reported never gets looked at.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.why_this_matters: The complaint is never answered. It is converted into a symptom, and you are sent to seek help for a reaction to someone else's conduct. What happened stays unexamined, and you carry both the harm and the label.
what_it_is: A reply to a complaint that talks about the complainant's mental or emotional state instead of the events.
Uses clinical-sounding terms such as anxious, paranoid or unwell, whether or not anyone qualified said them.
Often paired with an offer of kindness, such as a referral or 'we're worried about you', which makes it hard to object to.
Closes the matter: once it is said, nobody investigates the original report.
Found in workplaces, schools, clinics, care homes and family disputes where someone holds power over the outcome.
what_it_sounds_like: Have you thought about seeing someone about how you've been feeling?
I think this is your anxiety making it seem worse than it was.
We're just worried about your mental health, that's all.
A reply to a harassment complaint says only that 'we recommend our employee assistance program.'
A clinic answers a complaint about treatment with 'perhaps your distress is part of why it felt that way.'
Maybe you're not coping well with stress right now, and that's why you saw it that way.
A school letter on your report of bullying discusses your child's 'sensitivities' and says nothing about the incident.
what_it_is_not: A real condition can be part of the picture, and someone qualified raising it with care is doing their job. The question is whether the original report ever gets answered by anybody, or whether the diagnosis is where the matter ends.
A manager who offers support resources and also investigates your complaint.
A person who tells you they are worried about your sleep because they noticed you are not sleeping.
A clinician explaining a diagnosis you asked about.
A friend who suggests therapy and also hears you out.
A review that found the complaint was not supported by the facts and said so plainly, with reasons.
this_may_be_it_when: The reply to your complaint names no event, only your state.
The suggestion of help arrives before anyone has asked what happened.
Nobody investigates, and the referral is the only action taken.
The person offering concern is the person or system you complained about.
Your wellbeing is raised when you complain and not on other days.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The complaint is investigated and the support offered runs alongside it.
The suggestion comes from someone with no stake who also asks about the events.
You raised your own difficulty coping and asked for help.
A qualified professional you chose raises it privately, then goes back to your complaint.
Concern was voiced well before the complaint and has been consistent.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Distress and a real complaint often go together, and a caring person may attend to the distress first.
Staff are often trained to offer wellbeing resources whenever someone is upset, without any plan to sidestep the issue.
People afraid of conflict may reach for a soft-sounding suggestion because they do not know what else to say.
common_false_positives: A GP asking about your mood during an appointment about something else.
A workplace policy that sends everyone who files a complaint a list of support services, alongside the investigation.
A relative who notices you have seemed low and says so, before any complaint exists.
discernment_questions: Was my complaint answered at all, apart from questions about me?
Would the complaint still be valid if the suggestion about me were true?
Who is offering the diagnosis, and are they qualified and independent?
Does this arrive only when I raise something?
Is anyone examining what happened, now?
less_concerning_if: The complaint is investigated and the wellbeing offer is separate.
The person offering support has no stake in the outcome.
You are told what the review found, and why.
more_concerning_if: A diagnosis is entered in a file or shared with others in response to a complaint.
Your complaint is dropped on the grounds of your state, with no review.
Access to something you depend on, such as a role, placement or service, is made to depend on accepting the referral.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each new complaint is answered with a new concern about you.
Records about you begin to include notes on your state of mind, while the complaint is absent from them.
People who have heard about your complaint also mention your health.
You begin holding back reports to avoid the next suggestion of treatment.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.repair_check: Your complaint gets looked at on its own terms, with a written outcome, and any concern for your wellbeing is offered separately and without conditions. A sincere 'we're sorry you're upset' with no review of what you reported leaves the matter where it began.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.boundary_respect_check: Ask for the two things separately: help for you if you want it, and an answer on your complaint. Notice whether the second is quietly folded into the first. If an answer to your complaint arrives, with reasons, your request was heard.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.psychological_mechanism: People tend to treat concern for their wellbeing as kindness, and objecting to kindness feels ungracious. A clinical-sounding word can also make a complaint look like evidence of the speaker's state, so it gets weighed less. Over time the person may question whether their reaction was proportionate and drop the complaint themselves.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe feeling dismissed and then guilty for being angry about it. Some withdraw the complaint, avoid the service or workplace, or begin to treat their own distress as the real problem. A lasting wariness about asking for help can follow, even when they need it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the two: 'I appreciate the concern, and I'd like to look at what happened. Can you tell me how my complaint will be reviewed?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for a written answer: 'Please respond to the complaint itself, in writing, with what was found.'
response_options.disengagement: If a referral is offered in place of a review, set it aside for now and say you will take it up separately and by choice.
response_options.support_seeking: Take your account to someone outside the system, such as an independent patient advocate, an ombudsman or a union representative, who can help press for a response on the facts.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Put the complaint in writing, with dates, to a named person, and keep a copy. If it is answered with comments about your health, note that and ask for the outcome in writing.

Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.boundary_script: "I'm glad you care about how I'm doing, and I'll take that up separately. What I'd like now is an answer to the complaint itself: what happened on the fourteenth, and what will be done about it."
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.safety_note: This can sit next to real stakes: a diagnosis written in a file can affect work, housing, a care placement or custody. Watch for a label being recorded or shared, for help being made a condition of keeping a role or place, and for pressure toward treatment you did not ask for. Ask for copies of what is recorded, and reach an ombudsman, patient advocate, union representative or legal aid service.
misuse_warning: Not every suggestion to seek help is an evasion. Treating kind concern as an attack can cost you real support.
Saying a clinician is dodging accountability because they raised a diagnosis can shut out appropriate care. The test is whether your complaint was answered.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing turns your everyday limits and reactions into signs of a disorder; this one shows up at the moment of a complaint and ends it. Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown uses psychological terms like 'projecting' in a quarrel, whereas this uses a diagnosis-style reply, often in an institution, so that no review follows. Frame Assassination swaps the topic to your character; here it is swapped to your condition, and a referral becomes the outcome.
Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis.core_meaning: Answering a complaint about someone's conduct by suggesting the complainant has a condition, so the complaint is treated as a symptom.
